analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the government office created to collect financial data and spot risks in the banking system.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote, so the Office of Financial Research remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Office of Financial Research, the Treasury-based agency created by the Dodd-Frank law to collect data from financial companies and watch for threats to the financial system. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor. It sat in the House Financial Services Committee until that Congress ended, so the office was never touched.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, large banks and other financial companies would have benefited most. They would no longer face the Office of Financial Research's data-collection demands or help fund it, and regulators would lose the centralized research capability for spotting buildup of risk across the system — the kind of blind spot that preceded the 2008 crisis. Financial firms would save compliance costs; the cost would fall on regulators and, indirectly, on the public, which relies on early warnings of financial trouble.

how_it_helps.text: For the financial industry, the bill would have eliminated the Office of Financial Research, the new Dodd-Frank agency created to collect data from financial companies and monitor risks across the system.

The bill repealed the office's entire statutory foundation — subtitle B of title I of Dodd-Frank — and stripped every reference to it from other Dodd-Frank sections, so the office and its data-collection authority would cease to exist.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the public would bear the cost of losing an independent early-warning system for financial crises. Regulators would lose the data and analysis the office provided, and taxpayers would again carry more of the risk if hidden problems built up in the banking system unseen.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of repealing the office argued it duplicated data collection already done by bank regulators and would impose new reporting costs on financial firms — a cost those firms would have shed under this bill.

A repeal would have left regulators without a central research body, since the bill strikes the office not only from Dodd-Frank's title I but also from the Paperwork Reduction Act and related provisions, removing it wholesale rather than reforming how it works.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the financial industry, the bill's benefit was real but narrow: ending a new data-reporting regime and one regulator's budget. For the public, the cost would have been losing the government's dedicated office for detecting buildup of systemic risk — the kind of blind spot that preceded the 2008 crisis the office was created to prevent. On balance the bill traded a modest industry compliance burden for a meaningful loss of public oversight, and it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the Congress ended before it could go anywhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeb Hensarling introduced the bill on July 30, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still parked in committee.
Because the bill never passed, the Office of Financial Research, created by the Dodd-Frank Act to gather data on the financial system, was not repealed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Dodd-Frank framework and its backers came out ahead: the Office of Financial Research survived intact, and the financial industry did not get the repeal it sought. Nobody had to fight for that outcome — a single sponsor with no cosponsors was enough to bury the bill in committee.

for.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Office of Financial Research.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one cosponsored, so the only visible partisan signal is that a single House Republican sponsored it and no Democrat or other Republican joined.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed financial firms from the Office of Financial Research's data collection and monitoring, and from assessments that funded the office. The bill died, so the industry gained nothing, but its interest here ran against the public's interest in having regulators see systemic risks early.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators and the Treasury
industries.note: The Office of Financial Research sat inside the Treasury and supported other regulators with data and analysis. Repeal would have removed it; because the bill failed, the regulatory structure created by Dodd-Frank stayed intact.
